title: A School Is a School That…
author: Sylvia Duarte
summary: Sylvia Duarte recaps the Mid-Atlantic Hybrid and Microschools Forum held by the National Hybrid Schools Project, centred on the new Federal Scholarship Tax Credit that will route donations to scholarship granting organizations from January 2027. Founders are split: some want the money, others fear regulation and warn newcomers not to 'accidentally become a school'. The key legal question is what counts as a school, because the Treasury rule borrows Coverdell's circular definition 'as determined under state law', which could exclude homeschoolers and hybrid families in states that do not call homeschooling a school. Cato's Colleen Hroncich offers another reading, that state law determines whether a child receives a recognized K-12 education rather than whether a building is a school, which would include all homeschoolers. The piece adds survey data on what parents want and advice from West Virginia board member James Paul on preparing for scrutiny, and ends with the comment deadlines. It is a policy-oriented event recap with analysis, so Practice and Culture is the closest bucket.
points: The federal tax credit starts January 1, 2027 and funds only in states that opt in, with scholarship granting organizations free to set their own requirements.
The definition of 'school' borrowed from Coverdell is circular, and a literal reading could lock out homeschoolers and legally-homeschooling microschool families in about half of states.
Hroncich's reading is that 'as determined under state law' describes the education, not the school, so every state's recognized homeschoolers would qualify.
Research cited shows only about half of parents want five days a week in school and most homeschoolers left a previous school for push reasons, so families care less about labels than policymakers.
Paul's advice to founders is to define success on their own terms before regulators ask, help peer schools and invite legislators to visit.
quotes: Don’t accidentally become a school. Don’t accidentally become a daycare. Don’t accidentally become a summer camp. Because the whole reason you’re starting this thing…is because you don’t want the regulation or the box that a school might be defined as legally.
This is taxpayer money going directly to an SGO. It is not money coming from the state, from the local, or from the federal.
The newcomer homeschoolers are glad to take money. They’re glad to be tested, they’re glad to have the strings, because they’re coming out of traditional systems with tons of strings.
Instead, she reads “as determined under state law” as describing “education,” not “school.” What’s being determined under state law is whether a child is getting a K-12 education.
Saying “school means any school which provides elementary education” is a little like saying a cake is a cake that is baked.
I don’t know if the public has adjusted to the fact that only half of parents would want their kid to be in school five days a week
He also warned that new money brings new scrutiny, pointing to a recent ProPublica report in which reporters registered schools with just some paperwork.
Most people who are going to try to write rules for a hybrid school or a microschool probably never set foot in one.
